compute.reported_as: Fig. 3 shows the DMRG approximation E(|psi*_MPS>) for the (unknown) ground state energy of the transverse field Ising Hamiltonian (20) on a 20 by 20 square lattice, at a near-critical magnetic field strength of B = 3.0 and exactly encoded in an MPO with bond dimension D' = 22. [...] At bond dimension D = 2^15 = 32,768 our simulations already reached the maximum level of achievable accuracy within single precision arithmetic. [...] Figure 3. Convergence of the DMRG ground state energy per site as a function of bond dimension D for the critical transverse field Ising model on a 20x20 lattice, leading to an energy density of -3.18197(2). [...] The largest TPU configuration we used in this work consisted in half a pod (that is, 1024 cores). [...] Fig. 4 [...] if every time that we double the bond dimension we quadruple the number of TPU cores (see data points for D = 2^15, 2^16, 2^17 and 2^18 for 32, 128, 512 and 2048 cores, respectively), then the runtimes grow approximately only linearly in D. [...] We performed simulations with bond dimensions of up to D = 2^16 [...] We obtained converged results at these bond dimensions in just less than a day. [Free-fermion 10x10 run, not this row:] Results for D = 2^16 = 65,536 were obtained within roughly 23 hours on a slice of a TPU v3 pod made of 1,024 cores. We used seven sweeps and a Krylov dimension of 10
compute.source: Ganahl et al., PRX Quantum 4, 010317 (2023) = arXiv:2204.05693: Sec. V.B 'Transverse field Ising model' and Fig. 3; Sec. V.C and Fig. 4; Sec. VI Summary; Sec. V.A (free-fermion timing), arXiv:2204.05693 (compute pass 2026-09-16)
compute.note: bond_dimension = 32768 = 2^15 is stated for this TFIM 20x20 result (single-precision accuracy limit reached there; Fig. 3 also shows larger D). verified.note: Record row. Number, convention, class and bond dimension agree: the printed value is the energy reached at D = 2^15 (Fig. 3 plots D = 1024-32768, no extrapolation; the D = 2^14 point is -3.1819720), so variational with compute.bond_dimension 32768. Boundary conditions are not stated in the paper; open-open is established indirectly (card C3: the caption's own comparison with open finite-PEPS values at 11 x 11 and 21 x 21 brackets it, and it lies just below VarBench's open-boundary DMRG and MPS-RNN rows on this instance; any periodic direction would lower it by several 1e-3 per site). journal_read.note: Record row. Journal = arXiv v1: same caption value -3.18197(2), same B = 3.0, same D = 2^15 = 32 768 statement ("At bond dimension D = 2^15 = 32 768 our simulations already reached the maximum level of achievable accuracy within single-precision arithmetic"), same Lubasch et al. comparison (-3.172 10(1) at 11 x 11, -3.182 43(1) at 21 x 21, open PEPS: PRB 90, 064425 Table, read in this group). Journal Eq. (18) H = -sum s^z s^z + B sum s^x (arXiv Eq. (20), same sign): the sign of the field term does not change the spectrum (rotation by pi about z), no constant. Journal Fig. 3 main panel has six markers at D = 2^10 ... 2^15 (x ticks 102.56-281.57 pt, 35.8 pt per doubling), so no D = 2^16 point was added in review; variational at D = 2^15. Boundary still not stated in the journal text; open-open stays inferred (prior card C3; the bracketing by the open 11 x 11 and 21 x 21 PEPS values the caption quotes). Sigma: the (2) is a deterministic DMRG uncertainty, kept in method_detail per the settled VA6#7 entry. Own computation (primary). Not a duplicate: no other row on the instance carries -1272.788.

compute.reported_as: During the training, we use Adam optimizer with batch size 1,024 for all reported results, and we have found that the stochastic reconfiguration (SR) and the plain stochastic gradient descent (SGD) generally produce higher variational energies within the same number of training steps or wall-clock time. Gradient clipping with global norm 1 is applied to alleviate the energy spikes. After the training, each reported variational energy is estimated from 10^6 samples, and its statistical error is too small to be visible in the plots. [...] For bond dimensions chi <= 10, we use learning rate 1e-2 for 10,000 steps, 1e-3 for another 10,000 steps, and finally 1e-4 for 20,000 steps. We manually reduce the learning rate by a factor of 10 if we find the variational energy diverges in the middle of training. For bond dimensions chi > 10, we start from learning rate 1e-3. The training of a tensor-RNN with chi = 64 on the 10 x 10 triangular AFHM takes about 2 days on an Nvidia V100 GPU. || method string: "1D MPS-RNN (bond dimension = 64)"
compute.source: Supplemental Material Sec. S7 'Details of numerical experiments' (arXiv:2206.12363v2 = Phys. Rev. Research 5, L032001; published PDF checked, identical text), arXiv:2206.12363 (compute pass 2026-09-16)
compute.note: Blanket statement for all reported results. samples = 1024 is the Adam batch size per training step; the final energies are evaluated from 1e6 samples. The only device/wall-clock statement ('about 2 days on an Nvidia V100 GPU') is for the tensor-RNN with chi = 64 on the 10x10 triangular lattice, which is not the bond dimension of this row, so device/wall_clock are left null here. Step count is stated only for chi <= 10 (40,000 steps total); for chi > 10 only the starting learning rate is given. Parameter counts are shown only graphically (Fig. S3, energy error vs number of parameters), no number stated; static memory scales as O(V chi^2) for 1D/2D MPS-RNN and O(V chi^3) for tensor-RNN. bond_dimension is left null because the worklist's chi (40 for 10x10, 64 for the 20x20 TFIM) is not stated as a number in the paper text (Fig. 4 plots energy vs chi without a table; the 20x20 TFIM appears only in Fig. S4(b) with chi = 16). Worklist had no arXiv id; arXiv 2206.12363 read from the repo cache.
